source: In the S bus, in the rush hour. A chap of about 26, felt hat with a cord instead of a ribbon, neck too long, as if someone’s been having a tug-of-war with it. People getting off. The chap in question gets annoyed with one of the men standing next to him. He accuses him of jostling him every time anyone goes past. A snivelling tone which is meant to be aggressive. When he sees a vacant seat he throws himself on to it. Two hours later, I meet him in the Cour de Rome, in front of the gare Saint-Lazare. He’s with a friend who’s saying: "You ought to get an extra button put on your overcoat." He shows him where (at the lapels) and why.

gens.text: In the hospital's chaos, through the crowded triage, patients waited, chairs lining the walls. They shuffled forms, attaching colorful wristbands, while the intercom crackled with urgent calls. Two hours passed, the man's condition worsened, his friend fidgeted, eyeing the clock, hearts racing. Around them, three nurses coordinated, their steps quick, voices hushed, tending to the most critical cases first. The room hummed with tension, a blend of sterile efficiency and human despair, as the doctor checked a chart, the nurse adjusted a drip, and the world outside seemed distant. Yet, amidst the rush, a sense of calm prevailed, each action purposeful, every decision weighed against time. She glanced at him, her expression softened, "We're doing everything we can," she reassured, though the wait felt endless. He nodded, his grip tightening on the armrest, a silent plea for help.
